kernelIdea: a · 0 = 0 and a · S(b) = a + (a · b). Multiplication is built on addition exactly as addition was built on the successor.

kernels.l1: Three groups of two. Count them all up.
kernels.l2: Multiplying is adding the same number again and again. Three times two means two, and two more, and two more.
kernels.l3: Multiplication is defined by two rules: multiplying by zero gives zero, and multiplying by the next of something adds one more copy. So multiplication is built on addition just as addition was built on next.
kernels.l4: a · 0 = 0 and a · S(b) = a + (a · b). Multiplication is built on addition exactly as addition was built on the successor, so a · 1 = a is a small theorem and 3 · 2 = 6 is a derivation.
kernels.l5: The tower is successor, then addition, then multiplication, each defined recursively from the one below; the distributive law assumed throughout the course is provable from here.
kernels.l6: Every arithmetic law used earlier in the course — commutativity, associativity, distributivity — is a theorem of this system, provable by induction.
kernels.l7: a · 0 = 0 and a · S(b) = a + (a·b) build multiplication on addition as addition was built on succession; the distributive law assumed since Chapter 4 is provable here by induction.
kernels.l8: Nine axioms and two recursive definitions generate all of elementary arithmetic; Gödel showed that the resulting theory, if consistent, cannot prove every true statement about ℕ.
